h1: The IBD Diploma in Brewing and how to prepare for it
title: IBD Diploma in Brewing: How to Prepare | Craft Beer School
desc: What the IBD Diploma in Brewing covers, how its three modules work and a study plan that suits a working brewer in India.
teaser: The IBD Diploma is where brewing stops being a recipe and starts being science. Here is how to get ready for it.
standfirst: The Institute of Brewing and Distilling's Diploma in Brewing is the step up from the General Certificate. It tests whether you understand why the process works, not only how to run it. This guide covers what it involves and how to prepare while holding down a brewing job.
sections: The Diploma sits in the middle of the IBD ladder

The Institute of Brewing and Distilling (IBD) runs a ladder of brewing qualifications. The General Certificate in Brewing covers the process at a broad, practical level. The Diploma in Brewing goes deeper into the science and engineering behind each stage. The Master Brewer qualification sits at the top.

Most Diploma candidates already work in a brewery and have passed the General Certificate. Our guide to preparing for the IBD General Certificate in Brewing covers that first step. The IBD sets its own entry guidance, exam dates and fees. These change, so check its website before you plan around a sitting.

The Diploma in Brewing is split into three modules, each with its own written exam:

  • Module 1: materials and wort. Malting, adjuncts, water, hops, milling, mashing, lautering and boiling.
  • Module 2: yeast and beer. Yeast biology, fermentation, maturation, filtration and stabilisation.
  • Module 3: packaging and beer quality. Bottling, canning, kegging, pasteurisation, quality systems and flavour.

You can sit the modules at different times and the Diploma is awarded once all three are passed. That structure suits working brewers, because you can study one area properly before moving on. Many candidates start with the module closest to their daily job.

A brewhouse brewer often begins with Module 1, a cellar or fermentation brewer with Module 2 and someone from the packaging hall with Module 3. Starting where you already have context builds confidence. The first pass also teaches you how the exam is marked before you tackle less familiar ground.

The General Certificate asks what happens. The Diploma asks why and what you would do about it. Expect written answers that explain mechanisms and work through calculations. A typical style of question might ask you to explain how mash temperature affects fermentability, or to calculate the hop addition needed to hit a target bitterness, then discuss what would change the result.

That means rote learning is not enough. You need to understand, for example, that beta-amylase works best around 60 to 65 °C and alpha-amylase around 70 to 75 °C. You also need to explain why shifting the mash between them changes the final gravity. You also need the maths: extract, efficiency, alcohol from gravity, bitterness from alpha acid and utilisation.
A study plan for a working brewer

Most people preparing for the Diploma are working shifts. A realistic plan for one module spreads study over several months rather than cramming. A pattern that works for many:

  • Pick one module and get the official syllabus. Turn every syllabus line into a question.
  • Study five or six hours a week in short sessions, not one long weekend block.
  • Link each topic to your own brewery. If you are reading about lautering, go and look at your lauter tun and its numbers.
  • Work past papers under timed conditions in the final weeks, if you can get them from the IBD or a study group.
  • Write answers out by hand. The exam is written and handwriting speed matters.
Using your brewery as a textbook

The biggest advantage a working brewer has is access to real data. Your brew logs show extract, run-off times, fermentation curves and losses. Use them. If the syllabus covers brewhouse yield, calculate yours for the last ten brews and explain why it varies. If it covers yeast generations, track how attenuation changes from generation one to five.

This turns abstract topics into something you have seen. It also gives you examples to use in exam answers, which examiners tend to reward over textbook phrasing. In Indian breweries using rice or maize adjuncts, you have a ready example of cereal cooking and gelatinisation temperatures that many textbook examples skip.

Three areas trip up a lot of candidates. The first is the biochemistry in Module 2, especially yeast metabolism and the pathways that form flavour compounds such as esters, higher alcohols and diacetyl. The second is engineering: heat transfer, pumps, refrigeration and the maths behind them. The third is packaging for brewers who have never worked on a line.

These are exactly the gaps that self-study struggles to close. Reading the same paragraph on the Embden-Meyerhof pathway five times does not help much. Having someone explain it, then apply it to a stuck fermentation, usually does.

The Diploma is a respected qualification in large breweries and among technical brewers worldwide. It signals that you understand the process at a level beyond your own kit. For brewers in India who want to move into a larger brewery, a technical role or a head brewer job, it is a strong credential to work towards. It is not a shortcut to a job. Experience still counts for more on a brewery floor.

Your first step: download the current Diploma syllabus from the IBD website, choose one module and mark every line you could not explain to a colleague today. That list is your study plan.
faqs: How many modules does the IBD Diploma in Brewing have?
Three. Module 1 covers materials and wort, Module 2 yeast and beer, Module 3 packaging and beer quality. Each is examined separately and the Diploma is awarded once all three are passed.
Do I need the General Certificate before the Diploma?
Most candidates pass the General Certificate in Brewing first. Check the IBD's current entry guidance before you register.
How long should I study for one Diploma module?
Many working brewers spread one module over several months at around five or six hours a week, with past papers in the final weeks.
